Winter bans on sailing were a legal fiction, not a closed sea, p. 277; a voyage from Alexandria to Crete is recorded for December 1319, p. 294. Winter stays open and costs more risk. No sailing time was reached. The nearest recorded figure is one winter round trip from Genoa to Alexandria in 1369 to 1370, 81 days, pp. 297 to 298.

Sailing along the Levantine coast was generally interrupted in winter, and Venetians sometimes went to Egypt off season to buy cheaply, p. 119 n. 19. Venice traded with Egypt through Famagusta, which replaced Acre as the port of call, p. 133, and especially while Venice forbade direct trade, 1323 to 1344, p. 135.
Pegolotti lists Alexandria duties and freight, not sailing times; the toll is an estimate.

pp. 135 to 137: in 1323 Venice, under papal pressure, forbade trade with Mamluk lands; the halt in direct trading lasted until 1344; Venice sent an envoy in August 1344, the treaty of 1345 fixed the taxes and the galley service resumed in 1345 (p. 137 n. 116). Before 1345 the leg is not open. Sailing along the Levantine coast was generally interrupted in winter, and Venetians sometimes went to Egypt off season to buy cheaply, p. 119 n. 19.
